entity.name: Omar Khayyam
entity.description: The Persian poet-mathematician who calculated the solar year to six decimal places. Khayyam solved cubic equations three centuries before European mathematicians, designed a calendar more accurate than the Gregorian, and wrote quatrains that became some of the most quoted poetry in the English language through Edward FitzGerald's 1859 translation.

story.name: Omar Khayyam
story.description: A tent-maker's son solves cubic equations in Samarkand, builds an observatory in Isfahan, designs a calendar still used a millennium later, and predicts his tomb will lie beneath falling blossoms. The polymath who bridged Persian poetry and mathematics.

moments.name: Omar Khayyam Is Born in Nishapur, a Seljuk Empire Metropolis
moments.subtitle: A future polymath enters the world in a city that was once a center of Zoroastrianism
moments.description: On 18 May 1048, Omar Khayyam was born in Nishapur, a major metropolis in the Khorasan province of the Seljuk Empire (modern-day Iran). His surname means 'tent-maker' in Arabic, suggesting his forebears' trade. Khayyam memorized much of the Quran as a child and studied mathematics, astronomy, and philosophy under the region's leading scholars. His early tutors recognized exceptional talent and placed him under Imam Muwaffaq Nishaburi, who taught children of the highest nobility. After completing studies in Nishapur, Khayyam traveled to Bukhara around 1068 to study at the renowned library of the Ark, beginning a peripatetic scholarly career.

moments.name: Khayyam Completes His Treatise on Algebra, Solving All Cubic Equations Geometrically
moments.subtitle: Three centuries before Descartes, a Persian mathematician cracks the cubic
moments.description: Around 1070, Omar Khayyam moved to Samarkand and began composing his Treatise on Algebra under the patronage of the city's governor, Abu Tahir. Completed around 1079, the work provided the first general geometric solution for all types of cubic equations using intersections of conic sections. Khayyam catalogued 14 types of cubic equations that could not be reduced to simpler forms and solved each geometrically. This systematic classification anticipated the algebraic work of European mathematicians by centuries. Descartes later received credit for methods Khayyam had pioneered, making the Persian polymath one of history's most under-recognized mathematical innovators.

moments.name: Khayyam Measures the Solar Year to Six Decimal Places at an Isfahan Observatory
moments.subtitle: An accuracy so precise the answer would not change in a human lifetime
moments.description: Between 1074 and 1079, Omar Khayyam led a team of scientists at an observatory in Isfahan, commissioned by Sultan Malik-Shah I and his Grand Vizier Nizam al-Mulk, to reform the Persian calendar. The team measured the length of the solar year as 365.24219858156 days, accurate to the sixth decimal place. For comparison, the modern accepted value is 365.242190 days. The resulting Jalali calendar, introduced on 15 March 1079, used a 33-year intercalation cycle that was more accurate than the Gregorian calendar introduced 500 years later. A modified form of Khayyam's calendar remains the official calendar of Iran nearly a millennium later.

moments.name: Khayyam Undertakes a Pilgrimage to Mecca After Falling from Court Favor
moments.subtitle: A suspected freethinker walks to Islam's holiest city to prove his orthodoxy
moments.description: After the assassination of Sultan Malik-Shah I and Grand Vizier Nizam al-Mulk in 1092, likely by the Ismaili order of Assassins, Omar Khayyam lost his court patronage and set out on a pilgrimage to Mecca. According to the historian Al-Qifti, the pilgrimage was partly a public demonstration of faith to counter accusations of religious skepticism and possible Zoroastrian sympathies leveled at Khayyam by a hostile clergy. After the pilgrimage, the new Sultan Sanjar invited Khayyam to Marv as a court astrologer. Khayyam was eventually allowed to return to his hometown of Nishapur, where he lived as a recluse in declining health.

moments.name: Omar Khayyam Dies at 83 in Nishapur, Buried Beneath Falling Blossoms
moments.subtitle: The mathematician who predicted his own grave would be scattered with roses
moments.description: On 4 December 1131, Omar Khayyam died at the age of 83 in his hometown of Nishapur. He is buried in what is now the Mausoleum of Omar Khayyam. Years earlier, while visiting Balkh around 1112, Khayyam had predicted that his tomb would lie in a spot where the north wind would scatter roses over it. His disciple Nizami Aruzi visited the grave four years after Khayyam's death and found it at the foot of a garden wall, with pear and apricot trees dropping blossoms over the tombstone, exactly as foretold. The poet-mathematician's quatrains later became some of the most famous verses in the English language through FitzGerald's 1859 translation.
moments.address: Mausoleum of Omar Khayyam, Nishapur, Iran
